newsitem.title: CANADA: Falconbridge forecasts nickel supply deficit.
newsitem.headline: Falconbridge forecasts nickel supply deficit.

text.p: The supply of nickel in 1997 will probably not be able to meet demand, officials at Falconbridge Ltd said on Friday.
"We do forecast a deficit," Joe Laezza, vice-president of marketing, said in a conference call with reporters and analysts.

He said the company expected world demand for the base metal to total 925,000 tonnes, while supply would total about 916,000 tonnes. "At the moment I have to say I'm extremely bullish on nickel," he said.
The company expects a slight rise in production in 1997.
Nickel production in Norway should rise this year to 67,000 tonnes from 61,500 tonnes in 1996, said Lars-Eric Johansson, the company's chief financial officer.
Cobalt production from Norway should total 3,700 tonnes, up from 3,100 tonnes. Copper production should rise to 36,000 tonnes from 34,000 tonnes.

The Norway operation gets most of its feed from Falconbridge's Sudbury, Ontario operations, where 1997 nickel production should rise to 43,000 tonnes from a record 42,000 tonnes in 1996, Johansson said.
Production at the company's operations in the Dominican Republic should stay steady at about 30,000 tonnes of nickel in 1997, he said.
At Kidd Creek in Northern Ontario, zinc metal production should rise to 140,000 tonnes from 131,000 in 1996, while copper was expected to reach 118,000 tonnes from 99,000.
"It's a reasonable increase," Johansson said in an interview. "It's not spectacular but -- touch wood -- we expect to have a good production year with increases."
Falconbridge is in labor negotiations with its workers in the Dominican Republic, but company officials were optimistic a resolution would be reached soon.
"The two parties are pretty close at the present time, so we expect this will be solved in a short time," chief executive Oyvind Hushovd told the conference call.
He said union and company officials met with an arbitrator today. The 1,000 unionized workers' contract expired at the end of November. The main issue is wages.
